content: 1. Western blotting and line immunoassays should not be included in national HIV testing strategies and algorithms due to their complexity and cost. Instead, simpler and more cost-effective rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) are recommended to support the scale-up of HIV testing, prevention, and treatment services. 2. WHO recommends that all HIV testing algorithms achieve a positive predictive value (PPV) of at least 99% by combining tests with a sensitivity of ≥99% and specificity of ≥98%. The first test in the algorithm should have the highest sensitivity, followed by subsequent tests with the highest specificity. 3. Countries are advised to adopt a three-test strategy for HIV diagnosis when the positivity rate in national HIV testing programs falls below 5%. This ensures that individuals receive three consecutive reactive test results before being diagnosed as HIV-positive. 4. Dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests can be used as the initial test in HIV testing strategies for antenatal care to increase testing and treatment coverage. However, these tests should not be used for women with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART), women already diagnosed and treated for syphilis during their current pregnancy, or for retesting HIV-positive individuals. 5. Retesting individuals newly diagnosed with HIV before initiating ART is essential to verify their HIV status. This step helps to identify and correct human errors, such as mislabeling or device-related issues, ensuring accurate diagnosis. 6. Retesting individuals already living with HIV and on ART is not recommended, as it may yield incorrect results due to the effects of ART on the virus. However, for those who know their HIV status but have not started or discontinued treatment, retesting can serve as an opportunity to re-engage them in care and build trust with healthcare providers. 7. Early infant diagnosis (EID) is critical due to the high mortality rate among untreated HIV-infected infants in their first year of life. Virological testing using nucleic acid testing (NAT) is required to confirm HIV infection in infants, as maternal HIV antibodies can persist in the child up to 18 months of age, making serological testing unreliable. 8. Innovative approaches, such as point-of-care assays and adding NAT at birth (0–2 days), can improve the rapid identification and treatment initiation for HIV-infected infants. However, challenges remain in ensuring timely diagnosis and treatment due to delays in result return and losses in the testing-to-treatment cascade. 9. For children older than 18 months, serological testing is used following nationally validated algorithms, similar to adults. Facility-based testing is essential to identify children living with HIV, especially those born to mothers who did not receive interventions to prevent mother-to-child transmission. 10. Determining the exposure status of all infants and children presenting to key healthcare entry points, such as malnutrition wards, TB wards, and inpatient wards, and subsequently testing those identified as HIV-exposed, can increase case-finding. High-yield settings like these are critical for identifying undiagnosed cases. 11. Index-case testing, also known as family-based testing, has shown significant success in identifying children missed by infant diagnosis programs. However, efforts are needed to scale up this intervention widely. 12. The addition of NAT at birth to existing EID testing approaches can help identify HIV infection in exposed infants, particularly those infected prenatally. However, NAT results can be affected by maternal or infant ART used for postnatal prophylaxis, leading to false-negative results. 13. The ongoing risk of acquiring HIV during breastfeeding can delay the final determination of HIV status beyond 18 months. This underscores the need for additional testing throughout the exposure period to ensure accurate diagnosis and timely ART initiation. 14. The complexity of infant diagnosis has increased due to the scale-up of treat all policies, enhanced postnatal prophylaxis, reduced mother-to-child transmission rates, and the growing contribution of postnatal transmission. Infant diagnosis now requires a multi-step process with additional testing over the duration of exposure. 15. The optimal timing and frequency of infant testing depend on factors such as the timing of infection (prenatal, intrapartum, or postpartum), the sensitivity and specificity of the assay used, the mortality risk by age, and retention in the testing cascade.
